newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turks march against "state gangs" scandal.
newsitem.headline: Turks march against "state gangs" scandal.

text.p: Thousands of demonstrators on Sunday defied an official ban and marched through central Ankara to protest against a long-running security scandal.
An estimated 10,000 protestors banged on pots and pans, blew whistles, joined traditional folk dances and shouted slogans as they assembled in Ankara's main Kizilay square.

Police made no attempt to halt the march, but cordoned off the square on three sides, witnesses said. The protest, organised by the left-wing Freedom and Solidarity Party, had been banned by Ankara governor Erdogan Sahinoglu.
"Police, don't waste your time, catch the gangs," the protesters shouted.

The scandal erupted last November after a car crash revealed links among a fugitive right-wing gangster, a senior policeman, a government MP and a former beauty queen. All of the car's occupants, except MP Sedat Bucak, died in the crash.

A parliamentary enquiry into the "state gangs" scandal accused Bucak, who also heads a Kurdish anti-rebel militia, and former interior minister Mehmet Agar of deep involvement in a shadowy network of top officials and right-wing mobsters.
Bucak and Agar are members of Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller's True Path party.
"Ciller, Agar and Bucak must be punished," read one of the placards.

"Tansu Ciller told us to vote for her saying 'I am your mother, I am your sister' and then gave us these gangs. I am afraid for my children. The state should clear up the gangs," said Zeynep Kocak, one of the demonstrators. Ciller was prime minister from 1993 to 1996.

A court's bid to lift the parliamentary immunity of Agar and Bucak has been delayed for more than two months by the office of Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, who took office in a coalition with Ciller's party last June.
The car crash led to a series of revelations that right-wing gangs had been employed by the state to carry out political killings at home and abroad from the 1980s onwards.
The gangsters were also involved in drugs smuggling, arms trafficking and kidnapping, according to media allegations.
